The framework introduces a contract tuple 𝒞=(𝒫,ℐhard,ℐsoft,𝒢hard,𝒢soft,ℛ)\mathcal{C}=(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{hard}},\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{soft}},\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{hard}},\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{soft}},\mathcal{R}) that distinguishes hard constraints (safety-critical, zero-tolerance) from soft constraints (recoverable within a bounded window kk), paired with a recovery mechanism that transforms exponential compliance decay into linear decay (Lemma 3.10). The (p,δ,k)(p,\delta,k)-satisfaction definition (Definition 3.7) provides a probabilistic notion of contract compliance that accounts for the inherent non-determinism of large language model outputs, connecting agent behavioral specification to established PCTL model-checking semantics. We have implemented these ideas in ContractSpec, a YAML-based domain-specific language for contract specification, and AgentAssert, a runtime enforcement library, and evaluated them on AgentContract-Bench, a benchmark of 200 scenarios spanning 7 domains.

Summary of contributions.

The ABC framework advances the state of the art along six pillars, each representing a distinct innovation:

  1. 1.

    Hard/soft constraint separation. The formal distinction between hard invariants ℐhard\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{hard}} (safety properties) and soft invariants ℐsoft\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{soft}} (bounded-liveness properties with recovery window kk) enables nuanced governance policies that neither over-restrict agent autonomy nor under-protect safety-critical behaviors (Section 3.1).

  2. 2.

    Behavioral drift detection. The composite drift score D⁡(t)=wc⋅Dcompliance​(t)+wd⋅Ddistributional​(t)D(t)=w_{c}\cdot D_{\mathrm{compliance}}(t)+w_{d}\cdot D_{\mathrm{distributional}}(t) (Definition 3.12), grounded in an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck stochastic process model (Definition 4.1), provides both a lagging indicator (compliance drift) and a leading indicator (Jensen–Shannon distributional drift) of emerging misalignment. The Stochastic Drift Bound Theorem (Theorem 4.3) proves that contracts with recovery rate γ>α\gamma>\alpha bound expected drift to D∗=α/γD^{*}=\alpha/\gamma, with Gaussian concentration and a closed-form design criterion for the minimum recovery rate needed to meet any target (Dmax,ε)(D_{\max},\varepsilon) specification.

  3. 3.

    Real recovery. The recovery mechanism ℛ\mathcal{R} is not bookkeeping: it re-prompts the LLM with corrective instructions when soft violations are detected, achieving measurable restoration of compliance in real time (Section 3.4).

  4. 4.

    Compositionality. The Compositionality Theorem (Theorem 4.9) and its probabilistic extension (Theorem 4.11) establish sufficient conditions—interface compatibility, assumption discharge, governance consistency, recovery independence, and conditional independence—under which individual contract guarantees compose into end-to-end guarantees for multi-agent chains, with quantified reliability degradation bounds (Corollary 4.13).

  5. 5.

    SPRT certification. The Sequential Probability Ratio Test provides a statistically principled stopping rule for deciding whether an agent satisfies its contract at a target confidence level, enabling sample-efficient certification without fixed sample-size commitments.

  6. 6.

    ContractSpec and AgentAssert. The ContractSpec DSL (Section 5.1) provides a declarative specification language with a comprehensive set of structured operators and expressive predicates, while AgentAssert (Section 5) provides a production-grade enforcement runtime with sub-10ms per-action overhead (Proposition 4.15).

Key experimental findings.

Our evaluation across 7 models from 6 vendors, totaling 1,980 sessions, yielded the following principal results:

  • •

    The transparency effect. Contracted agents detected 5.2–6.8 soft violations per session that uncontracted agents missed entirely (0.0–0.3 violations per session in uncontracted mode). This is not regression; it is the measurement apparatus revealing violations that were always present but previously unobservable (Section 8.1).

  • •

    Hard constraint enforcement. Hard compliance C​(t)hardC(t)_{\mathrm{hard}} reached 88%–100% across all models under contract, confirming that the combination of training-time alignment and runtime enforcement achieves near-perfect hard safety guarantees.

  • •

    Drift prevention. In extended 12-turn sessions (E2), contracted agents maintained mean drift D¯​(t)=0.139\overline{D}(t)=0.139, with maximum drift bounded to Dmax=0.264D_{\max}=0.264 across all models. Uncontracted agents produce no measurable drift (no contract exists as reference). The D⁡(t)D(t) trajectory confirmed the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck mean-reversion prediction of Theorem 4.3, with drift stabilizing near the theoretical bound D∗=α/γD^{*}=\alpha/\gamma under sustained interaction.

  • •

    Real recovery effectiveness. Recovery re-prompting restored soft compliance within the prescribed window in 100% of violation events for frontier models (GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus 4.6), validating the practical impact of the linearization result (Lemma 3.10).

  • •

    Ablation. True ablation (E4) demonstrated that each contract component—hard constraints, soft constraints, drift monitoring, and recovery—contributes a 0.19–0.22 drop to the overall reliability index Θ\Theta, with no single component being redundant.

  • •

    Platform guardrail interaction. We documented interference between platform-level content safety filters (Azure DefaultV2) and application-level behavioral contracts, finding that overly strict platform guardrails block 40–60% of legitimate multi-turn conversations (Section 7.1.6). ABC operating under lighter platform filtering achieves equivalent or better domain compliance with zero false blocking, confirming that platform guardrails and behavioral contracts operate at complementary abstraction layers (Section 8.1).

Practical impact.

The ABC framework fills a critical gap in the AI agent governance landscape. Before this work, deployers faced a binary choice: operate agents with no formal behavioral guarantees (dangerous for regulated industries) or rely on platform-level guardrails that cannot express domain-specific compliance requirements and lack compositionality across multi-agent pipelines. ABC provides the middle ground—formal specification with runtime enforcement—that enterprise deployments require. The (p,δ,k)(p,\delta,k)-satisfaction parameters translate directly into auditable governance criteria (Section 8.4), the drift bounds theorem provides a closed-form design rule for the minimum recovery rate needed to meet any reliability target (Theorem 4.3(vi)), and the compositionality theorem quantifies reliability degradation across agent chains (Corollary 4.13), giving system architects the analytical tools to reason about end-to-end behavioral guarantees before deployment. The publication of AgentContract-Bench with 200 scenarios across 7 domains enables reproducible evaluation of future contract enforcement systems, establishing a shared baseline for the emerging field of agent behavioral governance.

Limitations.

We acknowledge three principal limitations. First, the current implementation relies on heuristic state extraction from LLM outputs to evaluate contract predicates; our experiments mitigate this via LLM-as-Judge evaluation (Section 7), but ground-truth extraction from unstructured agent outputs remains an open challenge. Second, our primary empirical evaluation uses the financial advisory domain as a rich test case combining safety-critical hard constraints with nuanced soft constraints; while we validate across 7 models from 6 vendors and the framework supports arbitrary domains via ContractSpec contracts, broader empirical validation across tool-calling agents, multi-modal interactions, and live production deployments is needed. Third, the LLM-as-Judge evaluation layer introduces additional API cost and latency; optimizing the judge pipeline for production-scale continuous monitoring is an engineering challenge that our current implementation does not fully address. A comprehensive discussion of limitations and threats to validity is provided in Section 8.2 and Section 8.3.

Future work.

Several directions emerge from this work. Guardrail coordination protocols—formal mechanisms for negotiating the boundary between platform-level content safety and application-level behavioral contracts—would resolve the interference we documented between Azure DefaultV2 and ABC contract enforcement, and would generalize to any deployment where multiple governance layers coexist. Formal verification of contract composition beyond serial chains—extending Theorem 4.9 to parallel, hierarchical, and cyclic multi-agent topologies—would broaden the framework’s applicability to modern agentic architectures such as those enabled by CrewAI (Moura, 2024), AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023), and OpenAI’s Agents SDK. Continuous certification via online SPRT—running the Sequential Probability Ratio Test in streaming mode against production traffic—would enable real-time contract compliance decisions without the latency of offline batch evaluation. Contract inference—automatically deriving ContractSpec specifications from regulatory documents, organizational policies, or observed compliant agent behavior—would reduce the specification burden on deployers. Finally, extending ABC to multi-modal agents operating over vision, audio, and tool-use modalities would address the growing deployment of agents that interact with the world through channels beyond text.

The core thesis of this paper is that autonomous AI agents require the same principled behavioral specification and runtime enforcement that traditional software has relied on for decades. Prompts are not contracts. Trust is not governance. Agent Behavioral Contracts close this gap: they make agent behavior formally specifiable, continuously measurable, and provably bounded—turning the current practice of “deploy and hope” into the engineering discipline of “specify, monitor, and enforce.”

Appendix A Full Proofs

A.1 Full Proof of the Stochastic Drift Bounds Theorem

We prove each part of the Stochastic Drift Bounds Theorem through a sequence of increasingly general arguments: a deterministic warm-up via Lyapunov theory, the stochastic extension via Itô calculus, ergodicity via the Foster–Lyapunov criterion, and finally the contract design criterion.

A.1.1 Deterministic Case (Warm-up)

Consider the deterministic drift dynamics

d​Dd​t=α−γ​D​(t),D⁡(0)=D0≥0,\frac{dD}{dt}=\alpha-\gamma\,D(t),\qquad D(0)=D_{0}\geq 0, (32)

where α>0\alpha>0 is the drift injection rate and γ>0\gamma>0 is the mean-reversion strength.

Lemma A.1 (Deterministic Stability).

The equilibrium D∗=α/γD^{*}=\alpha/\gamma of (32) is globally asymptotically stable, with explicit convergence

|D⁡(t)−α/γ|=|D0−α/γ|​e−γ​t.\bigl|D(t)-\alpha/\gamma\bigr|=\bigl|D_{0}-\alpha/\gamma\bigr|\,e^{-\gamma t}. (33)
Proof.

Define the error variable e⁡(t)≔D⁡(t)−D∗e(t)\coloneqq D(t)-D^{*} where D∗=α/γD^{*}=\alpha/\gamma. Substituting into (32):

d​ed​t=d​Dd​t=α−γ⁡(e+D∗)=α−γ​e−γ⋅αγ=−γ​e.\frac{de}{dt}=\frac{dD}{dt}=\alpha-\gamma\bigl(e+D^{*}\bigr)=\alpha-\gamma e-\gamma\cdot\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}=-\gamma\,e.

Consider the Lyapunov candidate V⁡(e)=e2V(e)=e^{2}. This function satisfies the standard requirements:

    V⁡(0)=0V(0)=0,

    V⁡(e)→∞V(e)\to\infty as |e|→∞|e|\to\infty  (radial unboundedness).

d​Vd​t=2​e⋅d​ed​t=2​e⋅(−γ​e)=−2​γ​e2=−2​γ​V​(e).\frac{dV}{dt}=2e\cdot\frac{de}{dt}=2e\cdot(-\gamma e)=-2\gamma\,e^{2}=-2\gamma\,V(e).

The Lyapunov ODE V˙=−2​γ​V\dot{V}=-2\gamma V integrates to V⁡(t)=V⁡(0)​e−2​γ​tV(t)=V(0)\,e^{-2\gamma t}, yielding the explicit bound (33). ∎

We now introduce stochastic perturbations, modeling the drift dynamics as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process.

Theorem A.2 (Stochastic Drift Bounds — Mean-Square Convergence).

Consider the stochastic drift dynamics

d​D=(α−γ​D)​d​t+σ​d​W​(t),dD=(\alpha-\gamma D)\,dt+\sigma\,dW(t), (34)

  1. (i)

    The mean-square error satisfies

    𝔼⁡[(D⁡(t)−α/γ)2]=(𝔼⁡[(D0−α/γ)2]−σ22​γ)​e−2​γ​t+σ22​γ.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl(D(t)-\alpha/\gamma\bigr)^{2}\right]=\left(\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bigl(D_{0}-\alpha/\gamma\bigr)^{2}\right]-\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\gamma}\right)e^{-2\gamma t}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\gamma}. (35)

A.1.3 Ergodicity via the Foster–Lyapunov Criterion

We now establish the existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution.

Theorem A.3 (Foster–Lyapunov Criterion (Meyn and Tweedie, 1993)).

Let {X⁡(t)}t≥0\{X(t)\}_{t\geq 0} be a continuous-time Markov process on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with infinitesimal generator ℒ\mathcal{L}. Suppose there exist a function V:ℝd→[1,∞)V\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to[1,\infty), constants λ>0\lambda>0 and b≥0b\geq 0, and a compact set C⊂ℝdC\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

ℒ​V​(x)≤−λ​V​(x)+bfor all ​x∈ℝd.\mathcal{L}V(x)\leq-\lambda\,V(x)+b\qquad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. (40)

Then {X⁡(t)}\{X(t)\} possesses a unique stationary distribution π\pi, and ∫V​𝑑π≤b/λ+supCV\int V\,d\pi\leq b/\lambda+\sup_{C}V.

Proposition A.4 (Ergodicity of the Drift Process).

The stochastic drift process (34) admits a unique stationary distribution π\pi satisfying 𝔼π​[e2]≤σ2/(2​γ)\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[e^{2}]\leq\sigma^{2}/(2\gamma).

Proof.

We use the Lyapunov function V⁡(e)=e2V(e)=e^{2} throughout for the convergence analysis. For the Foster–Lyapunov criterion, we require V≥1V\geq 1, so we define V~​(e)=V⁡(e)+1=e2+1\tilde{V}(e)=V(e)+1=e^{2}+1. Applying the generator (38):

ℒ​V~​(e)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\tilde{V}(e) =ℒ⁡(e2+1)=ℒ⁡(e2)=−2​γ​e2+σ2\displaystyle=\mathcal{L}(e^{2}+1)=\mathcal{L}(e^{2})=-2\gamma e^{2}+\sigma^{2}
=−2​γ​(V~​(e)−1)+σ2\displaystyle=-2\gamma\bigl(\tilde{V}(e)-1\bigr)+\sigma^{2}
=−2​γ​V~​(e)+(2​γ+σ2).\displaystyle=-2\gamma\,\tilde{V}(e)+\bigl(2\gamma+\sigma^{2}\bigr).

This satisfies the Foster–Lyapunov condition (40) globally (not merely outside a compact set) with parameters

λ=2​γ,b=2​γ+σ2.\lambda=2\gamma,\qquad b=2\gamma+\sigma^{2}.

By Theorem A.3, the process admits a unique stationary distribution π\pi with

𝔼π​[e2+1]≤bλ+supCV~=2​γ+σ22​γ+supCV~.\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[e^{2}+1\right]\leq\frac{b}{\lambda}+\sup_{C}\tilde{V}=\frac{2\gamma+\sigma^{2}}{2\gamma}+\sup_{C}\tilde{V}.

Since the bound holds globally, we can take CC to be any compact set containing the origin, and the tighter direct calculation from Theorem A.2 gives 𝔼π​[e2]=σ2/(2​γ)\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[e^{2}]=\sigma^{2}/(2\gamma).

This establishes part (i) of the main theorem. ∎∎

A.1.4 Gaussian Tail Bound

Proposition A.5 (Stationary Tail Probability).

Under the stationary distribution, the drift exceeds a threshold α/γ+η\alpha/\gamma+\eta with probability

ℙπ​(D>α/γ+η)≤exp⁡(−γ​η2σ2).\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\!\bigl(D>\alpha/\gamma+\eta\bigr)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\gamma\,\eta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right). (41)
Proof.

The OU process (34) has stationary distribution

πD=𝒩⁡(αγ,σ22​γ).\pi_{D}=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{\gamma},\;\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2\gamma}\right). (42)

For a Gaussian random variable X∼𝒩⁡(μ,s2)X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,s^{2}), the standard tail bound gives

ℙ⁡(X>μ+η)≤exp⁡(−η22​s2).\mathbb{P}(X>\mu+\eta)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2s^{2}}\right).

Applying this with μ=α/γ\mu=\alpha/\gamma and s2=σ2/(2​γ)s^{2}=\sigma^{2}/(2\gamma):

ℙπ​(D>α/γ+η)≤exp⁡(−η22⋅σ2/(2​γ))=exp⁡(−γ​η2σ2).\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\!\bigl(D>\alpha/\gamma+\eta\bigr)\leq\exp\!\left(-\frac{\eta^{2}}{2\cdot\sigma^{2}/(2\gamma)}\right)=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\gamma\,\eta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right).

This establishes part (iv) of the main theorem. ∎∎

A.1.5 Contract Design Criterion

Proposition A.6 (Minimum Correction Strength).

To guarantee ℙπ​(D>Dmax)≤ε\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(D>D_{\max})\leq\varepsilon for a prescribed tolerance ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), it suffices that

Dmax≥αγ+σ​ln⁡(1/ε)γ,D_{\max}\geq\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{\gamma}}, (43)

or equivalently, the correction strength satisfies

γ≥αDmax+σ​2​ln⁡(1/ε)2​Dmax.\gamma\geq\frac{\alpha}{D_{\max}}+\frac{\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}}{2\,D_{\max}}. (44)
Proof.

We require ℙπ​(D>Dmax)≤ε\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(D>D_{\max})\leq\varepsilon. From Proposition A.5 with η=Dmax−α/γ\eta=D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma:

exp⁡(−γ​(Dmax−α/γ)2σ2)≤ε.\exp\!\left(-\frac{\gamma\bigl(D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma\bigr)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\right)\leq\varepsilon.

Taking logarithms of both sides and rearranging:

−γ​(Dmax−α/γ)2σ2≤lnε⟺γ​η2σ2≥ln1ε,-\frac{\gamma\bigl(D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma\bigr)^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\leq\ln\varepsilon\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\frac{\gamma\,\eta^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}\geq\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon},

where η≔Dmax−α/γ>0\eta\coloneqq D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma>0. Solving for η\eta:

η≥σ​ln⁡(1/ε)γ,\eta\geq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\varepsilon)}{\gamma}},

which yields (43) upon substituting η=Dmax−α/γ\eta=D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma.

For the exact bound on γ\gamma, substitute Δ=Dmax−α/γ\Delta=D_{\max}-\alpha/\gamma into γ​Δ2≥σ2​ln⁡(1/ε)\gamma\Delta^{2}\geq\sigma^{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon) and expand:

γ(Dmax−αγ)2≥σ2ln1ε⟺γDmax2−2αDmax+α2γ≥σ2ln1ε.\gamma\!\left(D_{\max}-\frac{\alpha}{\gamma}\right)^{\!2}\geq\sigma^{2}\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\gamma D_{\max}^{2}-2\alpha D_{\max}+\frac{\alpha^{2}}{\gamma}\geq\sigma^{2}\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon}.

Multiplying through by γ>0\gamma>0 yields the quadratic

Dmax2​γ2−(2​α​Dmax+σ2​ln⁡(1/ε))​γ+α2=0.D_{\max}^{2}\,\gamma^{2}-\bigl(2\alpha\,D_{\max}+\sigma^{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)\,\gamma+\alpha^{2}=0.

The discriminant is (2​α​Dmax+σ2​ln⁡(1/ε))2−4​α2​Dmax2≥0\bigl(2\alpha D_{\max}+\sigma^{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)\bigr)^{2}-4\alpha^{2}D_{\max}^{2}\geq 0, and the constraint γ​Δ2≥σ2​ln⁡(1/ε)\gamma\Delta^{2}\geq\sigma^{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon) is satisfied for γ\gamma at or above the larger root, yielding (21). When σ2​ln⁡(1/ε)≪2​α​Dmax\sigma^{2}\ln(1/\varepsilon)\ll 2\alpha D_{\max}, a first-order expansion recovers the simpler approximate criterion γ≳α/Dmax+σ​2​ln⁡(1/ε)/(2​Dmax)\gamma\gtrsim\alpha/D_{\max}+\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\varepsilon)}/(2D_{\max}).

This establishes part (vi) of the main theorem. ∎∎

A.2 Proof of the Recovery Lemma

Lemma A.7 (Recovery-Augmented Compliance).

Let q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) denote the per-step compliance probability and r∈[0,1]r\in[0,1] the recovery effectiveness (probability that a violation is corrected within kk recovery steps). Then:

  1. (i)

    Without recovery: ℙ⁡[compliance over ​T​ steps]=qT\;\mathbb{P}[\text{compliance over }T\text{ steps}]=q^{T}.

  2. (ii)

    With recovery: ℙ⁡[recoverable compliance]≥1−T⁡(1−q)​(1−r)\;\mathbb{P}[\text{recoverable compliance}]\geq 1-T(1-q)(1-r).

Proof.

At each discrete time step t∈{0,1,…,T−1}t\in\{0,1,\ldots,T-1\}, define the events:

Vt\displaystyle V_{t} ≔{Csoft(t)<1−δ}\displaystyle\coloneqq\bigl\{C_{\mathrm{soft}}(t)<1-\delta\bigr\} (violation at step ​t​),\displaystyle\text{(violation at step }t\text{)},
Ft\displaystyle F_{t} ≔Vt∩{recovery fails within ​k​ steps}\displaystyle\coloneqq V_{t}\cap\bigl\{\text{recovery fails within }k\text{ steps}\bigr\} (unrecoverable failure at step ​t​).\displaystyle\text{(unrecoverable failure at step }t\text{)}.

Part (i). Without recovery, compliance over TT steps requires VtcV_{t}^{c} (no violation) at every step. Since each step succeeds independently with probability qq:

ℙ⁡[⋂t=0T−1Vtc]=qT.\mathbb{P}\!\left[\bigcap_{t=0}^{T-1}V_{t}^{c}\right]=q^{T}.

Part (ii). With recovery, we have

ℙ⁡(Vt)=1−q,ℙ⁡(recovery fails∣Vt)=1−r.\mathbb{P}(V_{t})=1-q,\qquad\mathbb{P}(\text{recovery fails}\mid V_{t})=1-r.

By conditional probability, ℙ⁡(Ft)=ℙ⁡(Vt)⋅ℙ⁡(recovery fails∣Vt)=(1−q)​(1−r)\mathbb{P}(F_{t})=\mathbb{P}(V_{t})\cdot\mathbb{P}(\text{recovery fails}\mid V_{t})=(1-q)(1-r) for each step tt.

The soft compliance guarantee fails if and only if there exists some step tt at which an unrecoverable failure occurs. By the union bound:

ℙ⁡(∃t∈{0,…,T−1}:Ft)≤∑t=0T−1ℙ⁡(Ft)=T⁡(1−q)​(1−r).\mathbb{P}\!\bigl(\exists\,t\in\{0,\ldots,T-1\}:F_{t}\bigr)\leq\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{P}(F_{t})=T\,(1-q)(1-r).

Taking the complement:

ℙ⁡(soft guarantee holds)≥1−T⁡(1−q)​(1−r).∎\mathbb{P}(\text{soft guarantee holds})\geq 1-T(1-q)(1-r).\qed
Remark A.8 (Tightness of the Union Bound).

Figure 6 illustrates the practical impact of recovery on agent reliability across models, confirming the theoretical bounds derived above. The union bound in Lemma A.7 is conservative because violations and recoveries create negative autocorrelation: a successful recovery at step tt makes compliance at step t+1t+1 more likely (the system has just been corrected). Tighter bounds using renewal theory yield an expected violation fraction of

(1−q)⋅𝔼⁡[τrecovery]𝔼⁡[τinter​-​violation]+𝔼⁡[τrecovery],\frac{(1-q)\cdot\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{recovery}}]}{\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}violation}}]+\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{recovery}}]},

where τrecovery\tau_{\mathrm{recovery}} is the recovery time and τinter​-​violation\tau_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}violation}} is the time between successive violations. This renewal-theoretic bound is tight as T→∞T\to\infty.

A.3 Proof of the Compositionality Theorem

Theorem A.9 (Deterministic Contract Composition).

Let agents AA and BB satisfy contracts CAC_{A} and CBC_{B} respectively, i.e., A⊧CAA\models C_{A} and B⊧CBB\models C_{B}. Under conditions:

  1. (C1)

    Interface compatibility: A handoff invariant IhandoffI_{\mathrm{handoff}} is maintained at the boundary between AA and BB.

  2. (C2)

    Pre/postcondition chaining: PostCondA∧Ihandoff⇒PB\mathrm{PostCond}_{A}\wedge I_{\mathrm{handoff}}\Rightarrow P_{B} (A’s postcondition plus the handoff invariant implies B’s precondition).

  3. (C3)

    Governance compatibility: GA∪GBG_{A}\cup G_{B} contains no conflicting governance constraints.

  4. (C4)

    Recovery isolation: RAR_{A} does not violate PBP_{B}, and RBR_{B} does not violate IAI_{A}.

Then Chain⁡(A,B)⊧CA⊕B\mathrm{Chain}(A,B)\models C_{A\oplus B}, where CA⊕BC_{A\oplus B} is the composed contract with:

PA⊕B\displaystyle P_{A\oplus B} =PA,\displaystyle=P_{A}, IA⊕B\displaystyle I_{A\oplus B} =IA∧IB∧Ihandoff,\displaystyle=I_{A}\wedge I_{B}\wedge I_{\mathrm{handoff}},
GA⊕B\displaystyle G_{A\oplus B} =GA∪GB,\displaystyle=G_{A}\cup G_{B}, RA⊕B\displaystyle R_{A\oplus B} =compose⁡(RA,RB,Rcascade).\displaystyle=\mathrm{compose}(R_{A},R_{B},R_{\mathrm{cascade}}).
Proof.

We verify each component of the composed contract CA⊕BC_{A\oplus B}.

Step 1: Preconditions. The composed system’s precondition is PA⊕B=PAP_{A\oplus B}=P_{A}. Since the environment satisfies PAP_{A} and A⊧CAA\models C_{A}, agent AA executes within its contract. This establishes the entry condition for the chain.

Step 2: Pre/postcondition chaining. Since A⊧CAA\models C_{A}, the postcondition PostCondA\mathrm{PostCond}_{A} holds upon AA’s completion. By (C1), the handoff invariant IhandoffI_{\mathrm{handoff}} holds at the boundary. By (C2), PostCondA∧Ihandoff⇒PB\mathrm{PostCond}_{A}\wedge I_{\mathrm{handoff}}\Rightarrow P_{B}. Therefore PBP_{B} holds and BB can execute within its contract CBC_{B}.

Step 3: Invariant preservation. The composed invariant is IA⊕B=IA∧IB∧IhandoffI_{A\oplus B}=I_{A}\wedge I_{B}\wedge I_{\mathrm{handoff}}. We verify each conjunct:

  • •

    A⊧CAA\models C_{A} implies IAI_{A} holds throughout AA’s execution phase.

  • •

    B⊧CBB\models C_{B} implies IBI_{B} holds throughout BB’s execution phase.

  • •

    IhandoffI_{\mathrm{handoff}} holds by (C1).

Therefore IA⊕BI_{A\oplus B} holds throughout the chain’s execution.

Step 4: Governance respect. The composed governance set is GA⊕B=GA∪GBG_{A\oplus B}=G_{A}\cup G_{B}. By (C3), this union is conflict-free. Since A⊧CAA\models C_{A} implies GAG_{A} is respected and B⊧CBB\models C_{B} implies GBG_{B} is respected, the full governance set GA⊕BG_{A\oplus B} is respected by the chain.

Step 5: Recovery composition. The composed recovery mechanism is RA⊕B=compose⁡(RA,RB,Rcascade)R_{A\oplus B}=\mathrm{compose}(R_{A},R_{B},R_{\mathrm{cascade}}). By (C4), RAR_{A} does not violate PBP_{B} and RBR_{B} does not violate IAI_{A}. Therefore recovery in either agent preserves the other agent’s contract state. The cascade recovery mechanism RcascadeR_{\mathrm{cascade}} handles cross-boundary effects by construction.

Since all five components—preconditions, postcondition chaining, invariants, governance, and recovery—are verified, we conclude Chain⁡(A,B)⊧CA⊕B\mathrm{Chain}(A,B)\models C_{A\oplus B}. ∎

A.4 Proof of Probabilistic Compositionality

Definition A.10 ((p,δ)(p,\delta)-Satisfaction).

An agent AA (p,δ)(p,\delta)-satisfies a contract CC if AA satisfies CC with probability at least pp, allowing behavioral deviation at most δ\delta from the contract’s nominal specification.

Theorem A.11 (Probabilistic Contract Composition).

Suppose agent AA (pA,δA)(p_{A},\delta_{A})-satisfies CAC_{A}, agent BB (pB,δB)(p_{B},\delta_{B})-satisfies CBC_{B}, and the handoff between AA and BB succeeds with probability php_{h} introducing deviation δh\delta_{h}. Then Chain⁡(A,B)\mathrm{Chain}(A,B) (pA⊕B,δA⊕B)(p_{A\oplus B},\,\delta_{A\oplus B})-satisfies CA⊕BC_{A\oplus B} with:

pA⊕B\displaystyle p_{A\oplus B} ≥pA⋅pB⋅ph,\displaystyle\geq p_{A}\cdot p_{B}\cdot p_{h}, (45)
δA⊕B\displaystyle\delta_{A\oplus B} ≤δA+δB+δh.\displaystyle\leq\delta_{A}+\delta_{B}+\delta_{h}. (46)
Proof.

Define the following events:

EA\displaystyle E_{A} ≔{A​ satisfies ​CA},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{A\text{ satisfies }C_{A}\},
EB\displaystyle E_{B} ≔{B​ satisfies ​CB},\displaystyle\coloneqq\{B\text{ satisfies }C_{B}\},
Eh\displaystyle E_{h} ≔{handoff preserves interface compatibility}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\{\text{handoff preserves interface compatibility}\}.

The composed chain succeeds if and only if all three events occur: EA∩Eh∩EBE_{A}\cap E_{h}\cap E_{B}.

Probability bound. We decompose using the chain rule of conditional probability:

ℙ⁡(EA∩Eh∩EB)=ℙ⁡(EA)⋅ℙ⁡(Eh∣EA)⋅ℙ⁡(EB∣EA∩Eh).\mathbb{P}(E_{A}\cap E_{h}\cap E_{B})=\mathbb{P}(E_{A})\cdot\mathbb{P}(E_{h}\mid E_{A})\cdot\mathbb{P}(E_{B}\mid E_{A}\cap E_{h}).

Under the conditional independence assumption—that BB’s behavior given correct input is independent of AA’s internal execution—we have:

  • •

    ℙ⁡(EA)≥pA\mathbb{P}(E_{A})\geq p_{A}  (by AA’s contract satisfaction),

  • •

    ℙ⁡(Eh∣EA)≥ph\mathbb{P}(E_{h}\mid E_{A})\geq p_{h}  (handoff success probability),

  • •

    ℙ⁡(EB∣EA∩Eh)≥pB\mathbb{P}(E_{B}\mid E_{A}\cap E_{h})\geq p_{B}  (by BB’s contract satisfaction, given correct input from a successful handoff).

Therefore pA⊕B≥pA⋅ph⋅pBp_{A\oplus B}\geq p_{A}\cdot p_{h}\cdot p_{B}.

Deviation bound. In the worst case, deviations accumulate additively across the chain. Agent AA introduces deviation at most δA\delta_{A} from nominal, the handoff introduces at most δh\delta_{h}, and agent BB introduces at most δB\delta_{B}. By the sub-additivity via union bound on the per-stage deviations:

δA⊕B≤δA+δh+δB.\delta_{A\oplus B}\leq\delta_{A}+\delta_{h}+\delta_{B}.

Extension to NN agents. By induction on chain length, for NN agents A1,…,ANA_{1},\ldots,A_{N} with handoffs h1,…,hN−1h_{1},\ldots,h_{N-1}:

pchain\displaystyle p_{\mathrm{chain}} ≥∏i=1Npi⋅∏j=1N−1phj,\displaystyle\geq\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{N-1}p_{h_{j}}, (47)
δchain\displaystyle\delta_{\mathrm{chain}} ≤∑i=1Nδi+∑j=1N−1δhj.\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{N}\delta_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\delta_{h_{j}}. (48)

The inductive step applies Theorem A.11 to Chain⁡(A1,…,Ak)\mathrm{Chain}(A_{1},\ldots,A_{k}) and Ak+1A_{k+1}, treating the existing chain as a single agent with composed satisfaction parameters. ∎

Remark A.12 (Tightness and Practical Implications).

The probability bound (45) is tight when events are independent, but conservative under positive correlation (e.g., when both agents benefit from the same favorable environment state). The deviation bound (46) is tight in the adversarial case but typically loose in practice due to cancellation effects. The NN-agent extension (47) reveals that reliability degrades multiplicatively with chain length, motivating the use of checkpointing and recovery mechanisms at intermediate handoff points for long chains.

A.5 Sample Complexity for (p,δ,k)(p,\delta,k)-Satisfaction Certification

A critical practical question is: how many test sessions are required to certify that an agent (p,δ,k)(p,\delta,k)-satisfies its contract? We establish a baseline via Hoeffding’s inequality and then show that sequential testing dramatically reduces the required sample size.

Proposition A.13 (Hoeffding Baseline).

To estimate the compliance probability pp within additive error ε\varepsilon with confidence 1−α1-\alpha using i.i.d. Bernoulli observations, the required sample size is

n≥12​ε2​ln⁡2α.n\geq\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^{2}}\,\ln\frac{2}{\alpha}. (49)
Proof.

Let X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} be i.i.d. Bernoulli(p)(p) random variables indicating per-session compliance, and let p^n=1n​∑i=1nXi\hat{p}_{n}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}. By Hoeffding’s inequality:

ℙ⁡(|p^n−p|≥ε)≤2​exp⁡(−2​n​ε2).\mathbb{P}\!\bigl(|\hat{p}_{n}-p|\geq\varepsilon\bigr)\leq 2\exp\!\bigl(-2n\varepsilon^{2}\bigr).

Setting the right-hand side equal to α\alpha and solving for nn:

2​exp⁡(−2​n​ε2)=α⟹n=12​ε2​ln⁡2α.2\exp(-2n\varepsilon^{2})=\alpha\quad\Longrightarrow\quad n=\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^{2}}\,\ln\frac{2}{\alpha}.

For ε=0.01\varepsilon=0.01 and α=0.05\alpha=0.05: n≥12​(0.01)2​ln⁡20.05=5000⋅ln⁡40≈18,445\;n\geq\frac{1}{2(0.01)^{2}}\ln\frac{2}{0.05}=5000\cdot\ln 40\approx 18{,}445. ∎

Proposition A.14 (SPRT Improvement).

Consider Wald’s Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) for testing

H0:p≤p0=0.90vs.H1:p≥p1=0.95H_{0}\colon p\leq p_{0}=0.90\qquad\text{vs.}\qquad H_{1}\colon p\geq p_{1}=0.95

with Type I and Type II error rates α=β=0.05\alpha=\beta=0.05. The expected sample size under H1H_{1} is approximately 150150–300300 sessions, representing a 60×60\times–120×120\times reduction over the Hoeffding baseline.

Proof sketch.

The SPRT maintains the log-likelihood ratio

Λn=∑i=1nln⁡ℙ⁡(Xi∣p1)ℙ⁡(Xi∣p0)=∑i=1n[Xi​ln⁡p1p0+(1−Xi)​ln⁡1−p11−p0]\Lambda_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ln\frac{\mathbb{P}(X_{i}\mid p_{1})}{\mathbb{P}(X_{i}\mid p_{0})}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[X_{i}\ln\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+(1-X_{i})\ln\frac{1-p_{1}}{1-p_{0}}\right]

and terminates when Λn\Lambda_{n} exits the continuation region (ln⁡β1−α,ln⁡1−βα)\bigl(\ln\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha},\;\ln\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}\bigr).

Under H1H_{1} (true p=p1p=p_{1}), the expected increment per observation is the Kullback–Leibler divergence

𝔼p1[Λ1]=KL(p1∥p0)=p1lnp1p0+(1−p1)ln1−p11−p0.\mathbb{E}_{p_{1}}[\Lambda_{1}]=\mathrm{KL}(p_{1}\,\|\,p_{0})=p_{1}\ln\frac{p_{1}}{p_{0}}+(1-p_{1})\ln\frac{1-p_{1}}{1-p_{0}}.

For p0=0.90p_{0}=0.90 and p1=0.95p_{1}=0.95: KL(0.95∥ 0.90)=0.95ln0.950.90+0.05ln0.050.10≈0.01671\;\mathrm{KL}(0.95\,\|\,0.90)=0.95\ln\frac{0.95}{0.90}+0.05\ln\frac{0.05}{0.10}\approx 0.01671 nats.

Wald’s approximation for the expected sample size under H1H_{1} gives

𝔼p1​[N]≈(1−β)​ln⁡1−βα+β​ln⁡β1−αKL(p1∥p0)≈0.95⋅ln⁡19+0.05⋅ln⁡(1/19)0.01671≈159.\mathbb{E}_{p_{1}}[N]\approx\frac{(1-\beta)\ln\frac{1-\beta}{\alpha}+\beta\ln\frac{\beta}{1-\alpha}}{\mathrm{KL}(p_{1}\,\|\,p_{0})}\approx\frac{0.95\cdot\ln 19+0.05\cdot\ln(1/19)}{0.01671}\approx 159.

The range 150150–300300 accounts for boundary overshoot and discrete-sample effects that cause the actual stopping time to deviate from Wald’s continuous approximation (Figure 7).

The optimality of this approach follows from the Wald–Wolfowitz theorem (Wald and Wolfowitz, 1948): among all sequential tests with Type I error ≤α\leq\alpha and Type II error ≤β\leq\beta, the SPRT minimizes the expected sample size under both H0H_{0} and H1H_{1}. This fundamental result guarantees that no sequential testing procedure can certify agent compliance with fewer expected observations than the SPRT. ∎

Remark A.15 (Practical Certification Protocol).

The SPRT reduction from ∼18,445{\sim}18{,}445 to ∼150{\sim}150–300300 sessions makes runtime certification practical for deployed agent systems. In practice, the test is run as a continuous monitoring process: each agent interaction constitutes one Bernoulli trial, and the SPRT statistic Λn\Lambda_{n} is updated incrementally. When the statistic crosses the upper boundary, the agent is certified; when it crosses the lower boundary, the agent is flagged for remediation. This sequential approach naturally accommodates non-stationary compliance rates via windowed or decaying variants of the SPRT.

Author Biography

Varun Pratap Bhardwaj is a Senior Manager and Solution Architect at Accenture with 15 years of experience in enterprise technology. He holds dual qualifications in technology and law (LL.B.), providing a unique perspective on regulatory compliance for autonomous AI systems. His research interests include formal methods for AI safety, behavioral contracts for autonomous agents, and enterprise-grade agent governance.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
